description: Take the White House apart in 3D and read its story: James Hoban's 1792 to 1800 Palladian mansion of Aquia Creek sandstone, burned in 1814, gutted and rebuilt in steel under Truman, and treated as a museum since Kennedy.

sections.alt: The south facade of the White House seen from the Washington Monument
sections.body: The President's House was a centerpiece of L'Enfant's 1791 plan, though his vision was for a grand palace five times larger than what was built. After L'Enfant's dismissal, Washington and Jefferson agreed on a design competition; nine proposals were submitted and Irish-American architect James Hoban, whose Charleston County Courthouse Washington had admired on a 1791 tour, won. On 16 July 1792 Washington reviewed the entries and "quickly selected Hoban's submission." Construction began at noon on 13 October 1792 with the laying of the cornerstone. Material and labor shortages shrank the design from three main floors to two, with brick lining the stone facades. Enslaved African-Americans quarried the stone while Scottish masons raised the sandstone walls; the total cost was $232,371.83. The porous Aquia Creek sandstone was whitewashed with lime, rice glue, casein, and lead when construction finished, giving the house its color and name. The public was calling it the "White House" by 1811, and "Executive Mansion" was the official name until Theodore Roosevelt's 1901 executive order. The persistent myth that it was painted white to hide 1814 burn damage is just that, a myth: the name predates the fire. One speculation ties the name to Martha Washington's girlhood home, White House Plantation in Virginia.
sections.caption: The south facade, built of Aquia Creek sandstone whitewashed when construction finished.
sections.credit: Ad Meskens, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: A competition for a president's house

sections.body: On 1 November 1800 John Adams became the first president to occupy the house. The next day he wrote to his wife Abigail: "I pray Heaven to bestow the best of blessings on this House, and all that shall hereafter inhabit it. May none but honest and wise men ever rule under this roof." Franklin D. Roosevelt later had the blessing carved into the mantel of the State Dining Room. Jefferson called the house too big but added, with Benjamin Henry Latrobe, the East and West Colonnades that hid stables and service buildings, the colonnades that still link the wings today. Jefferson also began the public traditions: house tours and a Fourth of July reception. It is a metonym for the presidency itself.
sections.heading: First residents

sections.alt: Benjamin Henry Latrobe's drawing of the White House
sections.body: On 24 August 1814, during the War of 1812, British forces set the mansion ablaze in the burning of Washington, retaliating for American destruction in the Canadas. Only the exterior walls remained, and most had to be torn down and rebuilt. White House employees and enslaved workers rescued the Lansdowne portrait of Washington; only three of the many looted objects have ever been recovered: a jewelry box returned in 1939 by a Canadian man and a medicine chest that had belonged to Madison, returned the same year by a Royal Navy officer's descendants. President Madison sheltered at the Octagon House while Hoban and Latrobe oversaw reconstruction from 1815 to 1817; James Monroe moved into the partially rebuilt residence in October 1817. The South Portico followed in 1824 and the North Portico in 1829, both built to Hoban's designs and carved by Italian artisans brought over for the Capitol. The North Portico's Ionic order carries a swag of roses carved between the volutes, linking it to the roses above the original entrance. The bow-fronted south facade may echo the Chateau de Rastignac in France's Dordogne, though the link is debated.
sections.caption: Benjamin Henry Latrobe's drawing of the house, from the reconstruction era.
sections.credit: Benjamin Henry Latrobe, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: The burning

sections.body: Inspired by Washington's open houses, the White House was open to the public from the start. The tradition peaked at Andrew Jackson's 1829 inauguration, when roughly 20,000 celebrants poured inside; aides lured the crowd out with washtubs of orange juice and whiskey. Open-house receptions continued until Grover Cleveland replaced them with a military review in 1885. Chester A. Arthur's 1882 redecoration brought in Louis Comfort Tiffany, whose 50-foot jeweled glass screen later divided the main corridor, and sold off over twenty wagonloads of old furniture at auction. The Harrisons originated the annual White House Christmas tree in 1891.
sections.heading: The people's house

sections.alt: Aerial view of the White House and downtown Washington, DC
sections.body: Theodore Roosevelt hired McKim, Mead and White in 1902 to strip out the Tiffany screen and Victorian additions, move offices into a new West Wing, and restore the neoclassical character. William Howard Taft added the first Oval Office in 1909 with architect Nathan C. Wyeth; Franklin D. Roosevelt later moved it to its present spot beside the Rose Garden. The West Wing burned on Christmas Eve 1929. In 1942 the East Wing was renovated to conceal the construction of the underground Presidential Emergency Operations Center bunker. By 1948 the timber-framed house, loaded with a fourth-floor attic and a new south balcony, was declared in imminent danger of collapse. Under Harry S. Truman the interior was completely dismantled and a new load-bearing steel frame built inside the original walls; the rooms were then rebuilt, the grand staircase repositioned, central air conditioning added, and two sub-basements, including a bomb shelter, dug. The $5.7 million job by contractor John McShain finished in 1952; the Trumans moved back on 27 March 1952. Truman had the original timbers sawn into paneling now found in the Vermeil, Library, China, and Map rooms.
sections.caption: The White House complex from the air: Executive Residence, wings, and grounds.
sections.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: The working presidency

sections.alt: The White House north front with a Secret Service officer
sections.body: Jacqueline Kennedy's 1961 to 1963 redecoration treated the house as a historic museum: Henry Francis du Pont helped recover original pieces, Paris designer Stephane Boudin of the House of Jansen gave each room a period theme, and the 1834 Zuber "Vue de l'Amerique Nord" wallpaper was salvaged from a demolished mansion for the Diplomatic Reception Room. Her televised tour aired on Valentine's Day 1962. In September 1961 Congress declared the White House a museum, barring the sale of its furnishings and ending 150 years of presidents auctioning off the contents. Every first family since has redecorated the private quarters under the eye of the Committee for the Preservation of the White House; substantive architectural changes to the Executive Residence have essentially stopped since Truman. Nixon built the press briefing room over Franklin D. Roosevelt's old swimming pool and added a basement bowling alley; Carter put solar water-heating panels on the roof and Reagan removed them; Obama reinstalled solar panels in 2013. On 20 May 1995 Pennsylvania Avenue was closed to vehicles after the Oklahoma City bombing, a closure made permanent after 11 September 2001, when the White House itself was briefly evacuated. In October 2025 the East Wing was demolished to make way for a new East Wing with a state ballroom over a rebuilt PEOC complex, slated to open in 2028.
sections.caption: The north front, photographed in March 2018.
sections.credit: Beethoven, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: The house as museum
In the cultural conversation
sections.body:
The single most famous image of the White House in all of film is its vaporization in Independence Day (1996), when an alien beam reduces it to fire and rubble; it made the building fair game for fiction. Roland Emmerich returned to demolish it room by room in White House Down (2013), while Olympus Has Fallen (2013) staged a parallel terrorist storming of the lawn and mansion. Tim Burton's Martians breached and burned it in Mars Attacks! (1996), a tsunami-carried aircraft carrier crushed it in 2012 (2009), and in X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014) Magneto drops a whole stadium around it as a barrier.

Television has given it two long-running counter-images. Aaron Sorkin's The West Wing (1999-2006) set 154 episodes primarily in the West Wing, the most sustained idealized portrait of the building ever made. In 24's seventh season (2009) terrorists take the White House through underwater tunnels, hold the president and over fifty hostages, and the building is retaken in a two-episode siege.

George Cooke's 1833 panorama The City of Washington from Beyond the Navy Yard depicts the White House at the left, rendered larger than life to balance the Capitol; in the White House collection since 1972, it has hung in the Oval Office under multiple administrations.
